food.text: In the Urnfield culture of Central Europe, which began around 1300 BC, farmers cultivated wheat and barley. They grew these alongside pulses and the horse bean. The culture is named for its custom of burying cremated ashes in urns in fields.

Salt production in the Salzkammergut region of Austria dates back to the Middle Bronze Age. In the 13th century BC, people there began mining rock salt underground in solid form, a major change from earlier methods.

The Bell Beaker culture is named after an inverted-bell drinking vessel used at the beginning of the European Bronze Age, arising as early as 2800 BCE. In central Europe the culture lasted only until 2300 BCE, when the Únětice culture succeeded it.

Although the Corded Ware culture (c. 2900 to 2300 BC) is often pictured as pastoral, evidence of sedentary farming emerged. At a site at Bronocice in south-east Poland, traces of emmer, common wheat and barley were found.
Millet and oats were cultivated for the first time in Hungary and Bohemia during the Urnfield period. Rye was already grown, but further west it was only a noxious weed.
The salt finds at Hallstatt extend to a depth of 215 meters below the surface. Wooden tools such as troughs were made in a completely uniform manner, which suggests industrial-style production.
Poppy seeds were used in the Urnfield culture, either for oil or as a drug. They were grown alongside the main cereal crops.
Flax seems to have been of reduced importance in the Urnfield culture, maybe because mainly wool was used for clothes.

art.text: The Nebra sky disc is a bronze disc about 30 cm across, weighing 2.2 kg, with a blue-green patina and inlaid gold symbols. The symbols are generally read as the Sun or full moon, a lunar crescent, and stars, including a cluster of seven stars taken to be the Pleiades.

The Nebra sky disc features the oldest concrete depiction of astronomical phenomena known from anywhere in the world. In June 2013 UNESCO included it in its Memory of the World International Register, calling it one of the most important archaeological finds of the twentieth century.
The Bronze Age golden hats are spectacular finds centred on Germany. The same region was also home to the central form of the Urnfield culture and to the Hallstatt culture.
The Nebra sky disc was found buried on the Mittelberg hill near Nebra in Germany in 1999. Archaeologists date it to about 1800 to 1600 BC and attribute it to the Early Bronze Age Únětice culture.

Similarities have been noted between Nordic Bronze Age imagery and the Nebra Sky Disc from central Germany, which is associated with the Únětice culture. This hints at links between artistic ideas in Central Europe and Scandinavia.

Two golden arcs along the sides of the Nebra sky disc, one now missing, are thought to have marked the angle between the solstices. An arc at the bottom with parallel lines is usually read as a solar boat with many oars, though some suggest a rainbow, the Aurora Borealis, a comet, or a sickle.

Axes and swords were buried with the Nebra sky disc, and birch bark in the sword hilts was radiocarbon dated to between 1600 and 1560 BCE. This matches the burial date, by which time the disc had likely existed for several generations.

Archaeologist Harald Meller has suggested that the Únětice culture had become a type of early state by the 20th to 19th centuries BC. In his view the Nebra Disc helped a ruling elite establish a new temporal order and demonstrate its claim to state power.

The creation of the Nebra Disc is thought to be linked to the 'prince' buried in the enormous Bornhöck burial mound in Germany. Dating from about 1800 BC, it is the largest Bronze Age burial mound in Central Europe.

Archaeologist Christoph Sommerfeld has argued that the Nebra disc encodes the 19-year lunisolar Metonic cycle. He says it is similarly encoded on the Trundholm sun chariot, from about 1500 BC, and the Late Bronze Age Berlin Gold Hat, which has a band of 19 star and crescent symbols.

war.text: Perhaps 4,000 warriors from Central and Northern Europe fought a battle in the Tollense valley in the 13th century BC. The remains of some 140 people have been identified, mostly young men aged 20 to 40, and the total number of dead is estimated at between 750 and more than 1,000. It is the largest excavated and archaeologically verifiable battle site of its age in the world.

Population density in the region was only about 5 people per square kilometer. A battle of perhaps 4,000 warriors would therefore have been the most significant known battle in Bronze Age Central Europe.
The Tollense battle seems to fit a period of heightened militancy about 3,250 years ago. Metal was becoming increasingly scarce north of the Alps, and populations seem to have moved.

In the 13th century BC, perhaps 4,000 warriors from Central and Northern Europe fought a battle in the Tollense valley in northern Germany. With a population density of only about 5 people per square kilometer, it would be the most significant Bronze Age battle known in Central Europe.

The Tollense battlefield lies in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern in northern Germany, along the small Tollense river. It was discovered in 1996, when a volunteer found a humerus bone at low water with a flint arrowhead embedded in it. Systematic excavation since 2007 has yielded thousands of bone fragments belonging to many people, about 13,000 by March 2018.

Radiocarbon dating places the Tollense battle between 1300 and 1200 BC. No clear traces of healing were found on any of the wounds, so the whole encounter seems to have taken place in not much more than a day. The victims were killed by a variety of weapons, including spears, clubs, swords, knives, sickles and arrows, and of the over 40 skulls found, many show battle wounds, one with a bronze arrowhead lodged in it.

The Tollense valley battlefield was discovered in 1996, when a volunteer found a humerus bone with a flint arrowhead embedded in it, and has been systematically excavated since 2007. Thousands of bone fragments from many people have been found there, including over 40 skulls, many with battle wounds and one with a bronze arrowhead inside it. Bones show cutting traces typical of swords.

In one spot in the Tollense valley, 1,478 bones were found within just 12 square meters. They may be the remnants of a pile of corpses or of a final pocket of resistance. Most remains are no longer in anatomical connection, and the victors probably threw the dead into the river, which carried them downstream.

A quarter of the Tollense skeletons show signs of healed traumas from earlier fights, including three skulls with healed fractures. This suggests that many of the men who took part were trained and experienced warriors. By contrast, no clear healing was found on the wounds from the battle itself.
It has been speculated that a better-armed group from the South or West wanted to cross the Tollense river on the way north or east. They would have used a strategic, long-established causeway.

The Tollense valley battle took place where the area had no towns or even small villages, and people lived on individual farmsteads. The closest known large settlement was more than 350 kilometers away.

One idea is that a better-armed group from the South or West wanted to cross the Tollense river on a long-established causeway, perhaps used for the tin trade. The battle seems to fit a period of heightened militancy about 3,250 years ago, when metal grew scarce north of the Alps.

The causeway at Tollense might have carried long-distance trade in tin and luxury goods. Pearls from the Persian Gulf were found near Halle, and Mediterranean glass pearls near Neustrelitz, both dated to 1200 BC.

science.text: For most of the 3rd millennium BC, arsenical bronze was the dominant form of bronze across Europe. Tin bronze later replaced it, and by around 1800 BC Central Europe and Scandinavia had fully adopted tin-bronze technology.
The Nebra Sky Disc comes from central Germany and is associated with the Únětice culture. Similarities have been noted between its imagery and the imagery of the Nordic Bronze Age.
Around 2100 BCE, metal production and exchange increased across northern and central Europe. Copper was imported from Slovakia via central Germany, while tin came from the British Isles.

The metallurgical influences from Central Europe are especially noticeable in the Nordic Bronze Age, most likely brought by people similar to those of the Únětice culture. Bronze tools appeared in Scandinavia shortly after 2000 BC, and bronze metalworking was adopted more systematically from 1750 BC.
The Pömmelte circular enclosure in central Germany was built by Bell Beaker people around 2300 BC. Close similarities have been noted between it and Stonehenge in Britain.

A triangular trade network linking Scandinavia, central Germany and the British Isles operated for a few centuries during the Late Neolithic (2250-1700 BCE). Its traces include straight-walled cups found in Denmark and central Germany or Bohemia, and Scandinavian flint axes found on the British Isles.
The number of copper artefacts in Funnelbeaker contexts decreases significantly between 3300 and 2800 BCE. They are almost absent between 2800 and 2300 BCE.

philosophy.text: The Nebra sky disc is a bronze disc about 30 cm across, inlaid with gold symbols for the Sun or full moon, a crescent and stars. It features the oldest concrete depiction of astronomical phenomena known from anywhere in the world. UNESCO added it to its Memory of the World register in June 2013.

Golden hats from Schifferstadt in Germany and Avanton in France, dated to about 1400 BC, may have been worn by elite religious figures that researchers call 'oracles' or 'king-priests'. The patterns on them are thought to represent calendars.

Large circular enclosures built around 2300 BC at Pömmelte and nearby Schönebeck in central Germany were important ritual sites. They remained in use until about 1900 BC, and Pömmelte is described as a central place of supraregional importance.

The archaeologist Harald Meller has suggested that the Nebra disc was part of the Únětice culture becoming an early state. He argues it allowed 'an extremely accurate positing of time' and represented 'the establishment of a new temporal order' by the ruling elite, demonstrating their claim to state power.

Christoph Sommerfeld has argued that the Nebra disc encodes knowledge of the 19-year lunisolar Metonic cycle. He sees the same cycle on the Trundholm sun chariot disc, dated to about 1500 BC. The Late Bronze Age Berlin Gold Hat, with a band of 19 'star and crescent' symbols, is also thought to encode it.

Gold discs from the Czech Republic, dated to about 1650-1250 BC, carry ornaments similar to the golden hats and are thought to represent simpler calendars. Some researchers suggest a Venus calendar is encoded on the Schifferstadt hat and on the later Ezeldorf and Berlin gold hats.

The Nebra disc was found buried in Wangen near Nebra in 1999. It only became public in 2002, when the finders tried to sell it and were eventually arrested after a sting operation in Basel, Switzerland.

Identical ritual objects from Haschendorf in Austria and Balkåkra in Sweden have been interpreted as solar calendars. The repeated use of the numbers 10, 20 and 30 in building them suggests a ten-digit counting system. Simple line-and-dot numerals on them served as assembly instructions.

culture.text: Around 2300 BC, large circular enclosures were built at Pömmelte and nearby Schönebeck in central Germany. These were important ritual sites that remained in use until about 1900 BC. Pömmelte is described as a central place of supraregional importance.

The Bronze Hand of Prêles from Switzerland dates from the 16th to 15th century BC. It has been described as the earliest metal representation of a human body part ever found in Europe. It may have been a ritual object, mounted on a standard, or possibly a prosthesis.

The largest known Early Bronze Age settlement in central Europe was built next to the Pömmelte enclosure. The remains of 130 large timber houses have been found there. They were typically 20 metres long, with some reaching 30.5 metres.
A gold axe and jewellery dating to about 1800 BC were discovered at Dieskau in Germany. They are thought to be associated with the ruler buried in the Bornhöck mound.

Tumulus culture societies traded with Scandinavia, Atlantic Europe, the Mediterranean region and the Aegean, exchanging items such as amber and metal artefacts. From the start of the Middle Bronze Age there is evidence for weighed metal being used as a form of payment or money. Weighing equipment has been found in central Europe from about 1400 BC onwards.
The Bronze Hand of Prêles was found in a grave along with a bronze hair-ring, pin and dagger. The hand had a golden bracelet or cuff decorated with solar motifs.

The patterns on the Schifferstadt hat are thought to represent a calendar, as on the later and more elaborate Berlin Gold Hat. The Berlin hat may encode knowledge of the luni-solar Metonic cycle. Some researchers have suggested that a Venus calendar is encoded on the Schifferstadt hat.

In Switzerland, a large ceremonial axe called the Thun-Renzenbühl axe was inlaid with gold decorations using a damascening technique. The same technique is known from gold-decorated weapons in Mycenaean Greece. A similar gold-inlaid axe was found in a hoard at Trassem in Germany, dating to about 1600 BC.

The cremation rite of the Urnfield culture is commonly believed to have originated in Hungary, where it was widespread since the first half of the second millennium BC. Some cremations also begin to be found in the Proto-Lusatian and Trzciniec cultures.

Ritual objects from Haschendorf in Austria and Balkåkra in Sweden have been interpreted as solar calendars. Simple numerals in the form of lines and dots on them represent assembly instructions. The repeated use of the numbers 10, 20 and 30 suggests a ten-digit system.
